posts.title: Week 1 — Introduction to Multisensory VR
posts.preview: First observations on presence, perception, and what changes when a virtual world begins to engage more than sight and sound.

content.text: This first week introduced the central question of the course: what makes a virtual experience feel embodied? I began by paying attention to the gap between seeing an environment and feeling located inside it.

I tested a simple scene while changing one sensory cue at a time—spatial sound, controller vibration, and small shifts in visual scale. Even subtle feedback changed how I moved and where I directed my attention.

content.alt: Animated documentation from the Week 1 VR experiment
content.caption: Week 1 experiment documentation.

content.text: Presence is not only something we see; it is something the body continually negotiates.
My main takeaway was that coherence matters more than intensity. A quiet vibration at exactly the right moment can be more convincing than a dramatic effect that is disconnected from the action.

posts.title: Week 2 — Backrooms Prototype
posts.preview: Building an uneasy liminal space through repetition, fluorescent hum, uncertain scale, and restrained haptic feedback.

content.text: This week I built a small Backrooms-inspired prototype to explore how sensory repetition can create tension. The scene uses nearly identical corridors, ambiguous landmarks, and a sound bed that never quite settles.

The experience is less about being chased and more about anticipating that something might happen. I wanted the architecture itself to feel unreliable, using familiar office materials in an arrangement that resists orientation.

content.alt: Abstract placeholder for the Backrooms prototype
content.caption: Early corridor study. Replace with a prototype screenshot.

content.text: I started with a modular wall and ceiling system, then introduced slight inconsistencies in room proportions. A low electrical hum is spatialized around the ceiling lights. Brief controller pulses occur near visual glitches, connecting the body's sense of touch to the environment's instability.
The restrained audio created more tension than the louder tests. Players also slowed down when rooms differed only slightly, suggesting that subtle variation encouraged careful observation.
The initial haptic effect was too frequent and quickly became predictable. Some corridor turns were also tight enough to produce discomfort, so the spatial layout needs another pass.
Next I will test longer quiet intervals, widen the circulation paths, and add one environmental interaction that changes the soundscape without explaining exactly what happened.
